'''Ian Lowe''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AO}} (born 3 November 1942) is an Australian academic and writer focused on [[environmental issues]]. A [[physics]] graduate, he is an Emeritus Professor of [[Science and technology studies|Science, Technology and Society]] and former Head of the School of Science at [[Griffith University]]. He is also an adjunct professor at [[Sunshine Coast University]] and [[Flinders University]].

Lowe has authored or co-authored 10 books, 10 Open University books, more than 50 book chapters and over 500 other publications. Books by Lowe include ''[[A Big Fix]]'', ''[[Reaction Time (book)|Reaction Time]]'',  ''[[Living in the Hothouse]]'', ''Why vs Why: Nuclear Power'', ''A Voice of Reason: Reflections on Australia'', ''Bigger or Better? Australia's Population Debate'', ''The Lucky Country? Reinventing Australia'' and ''Long Half-life: The Nuclear Industry in Australia''.

==Career==
In 1996, Lowe was chair-person of the advisory council producing the first national report on the state of Australia's environment.  He is a patron of [[Sustainable Population Australia]].<ref>[http://www.population.org.au/index.php/about-us/aims-a-objectives/139-aims-and-objectives Sustainable Population Australia - Aims and Objectives] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615035832/http://www.population.org.au/index.php/about-us/aims-a-objectives/139-aims-and-objectives |date=15 June 2011 }}</ref> One of his principal interests is the way policy decisions influence use of science and technology, especially in the fields of energy and environment.

He wrote for 13 years a regular column for ''[[New Scientist]]'' and also writes for several other publications, as well as contributing frequently to electronic media programs.<ref name=Lowe/>

Lowe was a member of the Australian Radiation Health and Safety Advisory Council from 2002 to 2014 and a former member or chair of many other bodies advising all three levels of government in Australia.

He was President of the Australian Conservation Foundation from 2004 to 2014.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wheelercentre.com/people/ian-lowe|title=Ian Lowe}}</ref>

In April 2015 Lowe was appointed to the Expert Advisory Committee for the [[Nuclear Fuel Cycle Royal Commission]] in South Australia.

He is currently Emeritus Professor of [[Science and technology studies|Science, Technology and Society]] and former Head of the School of Science at [[Griffith University]]. He is also an adjunct professor at [[Sunshine Coast University]] and [[Flinders University]].

== Energy advocacy ==
Lowe sees the [[nuclear power]] option for electricity generation as being risky and unworkable. He says nuclear power installations peaked last century and in the past 20 years, retirements, cancellations and deferments have outnumbered new reactor construction.<ref name="lowenuke" /> Lowe says nuclear power is too expensive, with insurmountable problems associated with waste disposal and weapons proliferation. It is also not a fast enough response to [[climate change mitigation|address climate change]]. Lowe advocates for [[renewable energy]] which he claims is "quicker, less expensive and less dangerous than nuclear".<ref name="lowenuke">{{cite web |url=https://www.theage.com.au/politics/federal/no-nukes-now-or-ever-20110319-1c1ed.html |title=No nukes now, or ever |author=Ian Lowe  |date=20 March 2011 |work=The Age }}</ref><ref name="lowenuketrans">{{cite web |url=https://www.abc.net.au/radionational/programs/scienceshow/should-nuclear-power-be-part-of-the-energy-transition/13587876 |title=Should nuclear power be part of the energy transition? |author=Ian Lowe  |date=16 October 2021 |work=ABC Science Show }}</ref>
==Awards==
Lowe was made an Officer of the [[Order of Australia]] in 2001 for services to science, technology, and the environment. In 2002 he was awarded a [[Centenary Medal]] for contributions to environmental science and won the [[Eureka Prize]] for promotion of science. His contributions have also been recognised by the Prime Minister's Environment Award for Outstanding Individual Achievement, the Queensland Premier's Millennium Award for Excellence in Science and the [[University of NSW]] Alumni Award for achievement in science. Lowe was named Humanist of the Year in 1988.<ref name="Lowe">He was awarded the Konrad Lorenz Gold Medal by the [[International Academy of Science]] in 2009.[http://www.naturaledgeproject.net/TNEPPatronIanLowe.aspx Professor Ian Lowe] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171017202145/http://www.naturaledgeproject.net/TNEPPatronIanLowe.aspx|date=17 October 2017}}</ref> He was President of the Australian Conservation Foundation from 2004 to April 2014. In 2009 the International Academy of Sciences, Health and Ecology awarded him the Konrad Lorenz Gold Medal. In 2019, the University of New South Wales recognised his body of published work by the award of a higher doctorate, Doctor of Science [D.Sc.].
